content: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends routine vaccination against shingles for all individuals aged 60 years and older. This recommendation is based on the fact that immunity to the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) decreases with age, putting the elderly population at higher risk. In the United States, more than one million cases of shingles (herpes zoster) are estimated to occur annually. Over 50% of individuals who live beyond the age of 85 will develop shingles at some point, and approximately 20% of these patients will experience postherpetic neuralgia, a chronic and often debilitating pain condition. The shingles vaccine has been shown to be effective. Thirteen years after vaccination, it reduces the incidence of shingles by 51% and decreases the occurrence of postherpetic neuralgia by 66%. The live attenuated vaccine does not cause acute shingles in vaccinated individuals. If lesions do occur, they are caused by the patient’s own native strain of the virus, not the vaccine strain. Reducing the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia is particularly important. While antiviral therapy can lessen the severity and duration of a shingles episode, it does not prevent postherpetic neuralgia. Similarly, steroids do not clearly prevent postherpetic neuralgia, though they may provide some pain relief during an acute episode when used in conjunction with antiviral medications. The vaccine, however, prevents postherpetic neuralgia and improves the quality of life for vaccinated elderly individuals. Zostavax, manufactured by Merck, is currently the only shingles vaccine available. It was approved by the FDA in May 2006 for the prevention of herpes zoster in individuals aged 60 and older. The vaccine must be stored frozen at all times until it is administered. At present, no booster dose is recommended. Zostavax is distinct from the chickenpox vaccine (Varivax) and should not be used as a substitute. Zostavax is 14 times more potent than Varivax, although both are live attenuated vaccines derived from the same viral strain. Individuals with a history of shingles can still receive the vaccine, as recurrent shingles has been documented in immunocompetent individuals. The vaccine can also be administered to people who do not recall having chickenpox during childhood. Serological testing to determine varicella immunity is not required prior to vaccination. There are specific contraindications to receiving the shingles vaccine. These include active cancer treatment with chemotherapy or radiation, leukemia, lymphoma, organ transplantation, active tuberculosis, pregnancy or breastfeeding, severe allergies to gelatin, neomycin, or any vaccine component, and immunodeficiency conditions such as AIDS or other congenital or acquired cellular immunodeficiencies. However, a history of treated cancer, including leukemia or lymphoma, is not a contraindication. Additionally, humoral immunodeficiency is not a contraindication to vaccination. There is no upper age limit for vaccination, and common medical conditions such as diabetes or heart failure do not preclude vaccination with Zostavax. For individuals taking anti-herpes medications such as Zovirax, these medications should be discontinued at least 24 hours prior to receiving Zostavax and should not be restarted until 14 days after vaccination. The cost of the shingles vaccine is approximately $155 per dose. In comparison, outpatient treatment for shingles costs around $200, while hospitalization for acute shingles can range from $3,221 to $7,206. Evidence suggests that shingles vaccination is as cost-effective as other public health interventions. However, most insurance companies do not cover the cost of Zostavax. In several states, only licensed medical doctors are authorized to administer the vaccine, which adds to the cost and inconvenience. Patients are often required to purchase the vaccine from a pharmacy, transport it on ice, and bring it to their physician for subcutaneous administration.
